slides: Before you practice, here's a quick summary of primes and factors. Everything important, in a few minutes.

slides.say: A prime has exactly two divisors, one and itself. One is not prime, and neither are zero and the negative numbers. Two is prime, and it's the only even prime.

Know the primes up to forty by heart. Two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-three, twenty-nine, thirty-one and thirty-seven. And ninety-seven, the largest two-digit prime.

All the other primes are odd. Odd plus odd is even, and odd minus odd is even too. So if two primes give an odd sum or an odd difference, one of them is two. Seventy-three as a sum of two primes? Two plus seventy-one.

To test a number, divide it by the primes up to its square root, and no further. Watch out for the fakes. For three, add the digits, like sixty-nine, six plus nine is fifteen. And never forget to try seven, like seventy-seven, which is seven times eleven.

Every number that isn't prime breaks into primes, in only one way. And it's divisible by every combination of its prime factors. Forty-four is two times two times eleven, so it divides by two, four, eleven, twenty-two and forty-four.
Is a number a divisor? Break it into primes too, and check that every prime is there, enough times. Unpack pieces like six or ten squared first.
Most questions just break a number apart, or build numbers from pieces, and look for the missing prime.

For a common divisor, we need factors that fit inside both numbers. For a common multiple, we need a number large enough to contain both sets of factors. The greatest common divisor is the largest number that divides both numbers. It takes each shared prime at its lower power. The least common multiple, the LCM, is the smallest positive number divisible by both numbers. It takes every prime at its higher power.

Forty-eight is two to the power of four times three, and sixty is two squared times three times five. The GCD is two squared times three, which is twelve. The LCM takes two to the power of four, three and five, and sixteen times fifteen is sixteen times ten, a hundred sixty, plus half of that, eighty. Two hundred forty.
The trap is just multiplying the two numbers, which counts a shared prime twice. And the GCD times the LCM is the two numbers multiplied.
The number of divisors? Add one to each exponent, and multiply. Two to the power of four times three has five times two, which is ten divisors.
Divisors come in pairs, so only a perfect square has an odd number of them. And exactly three divisors means a prime squared, like four or a hundred twenty-one.

The extra multiplier must complete every unpaired prime factor. We choose the smallest multiplier that does that. In a perfect square, every exponent is even. Twenty k a square? Twenty is two squared times five, so it needs one more five. k is five, and twenty times five is a hundred, ten squared.

And an equation in primes? Break the number, then match the exponents. Two to the power of a, times three to the power of b, is a hundred forty-four. That's sixteen times nine, which is two to the power of four times three squared, so a is four and b is two.
A prime can't be split between factors, one of them holds it whole.
And when the primes are letters, plug in the smallest primes in the right order, and knock out three choices before you mark one.

Before each question, ask yourself. Did I break every number into primes? Is it really prime, did I try up to the root, and seven? An odd sum or difference, is one of them two? GCD or LCM, lower power or higher power?
The common traps are calling one a prime, forgetting two, and multiplying instead of taking the LCM. [pause] That's it. Now go practice, and I'll see you in the next video.
